explanation: In some tellings, Arthur draws a different sword from a stone and later receives Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake. Durendal, Joyeuse and Tizona belonged to Roland, Charlemagne and El Cid.

claims.text: In Arthurian legend, King Arthur's sword is called Excalibur.
Durendal, Joyeuse and Tizona are the legendary swords of Roland, Charlemagne and El Cid.
In some versions of the legend, such as Malory's, the sword Arthur draws from the stone is different from Excalibur, which the Lady of the Lake gives him.

results.title: Thomas Malory: Le Morte d'Arthur - Students

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Short answer: the sources I found say Malory's stone sword and the lake sword are two different swords, but they disagree on whether he calls both Excalibur. The sword from the stone is broken in battle, and Arthur then gets a replacement from the Lady of the Lake. In some tales, this is his only sword. In most variants, this sword was then broken, and he receives from The Lady of the Lake a new sword called Excalibur.

claimResults.note: Search 5: in Malory the sword from the stone breaks and the Lady of the Lake gives Arthur a new sword, Excalibur, so the swords are distinct. The summary reports that sources differ on whether Malory also calls the stone sword Excalibur; that does not touch the claim, which identifies Excalibur as the Lady's sword. Counts at Tier B.

issues.note: Malory also calls the sword from the stone 'Excalibur' before it breaks (Wikipedia, King Pellinore; Britannica Students), so 'such as Malory's' in c3 is a loose example. The player-facing 'In some tellings' line is accurate; the Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin would be the cleaner example in the claim.

evidence.restatement: Durendal is Roland's sword, Joyeuse is Charlemagne's and Tizona is El Cid's.
In Malory, Arthur pulls a sword from the stone and later receives Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake, as two separate swords.
